profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-sized asset management firm between the research lead and the product manager responsible for turning the firm's experimental 3S-Trader framework into a client-facing pilot for the discretionary equities desk. The context is that the team has approval to run a six-week internal pilot using DJIA names plus one sector basket, and this meeting is to lock the implementation plan for the pilot package that will be shown to portfolio managers and compliance reviewers. The agenda is to align on what the 'pilot' will include, what artifacts need to be produced each week, who owns the scoring/strategy/selection workflow versus packaging and stakeholder communication, and what the timeline means for the first usable output. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan covering the pilot scope, weekly deliverables, ownership split, and the date of the first reviewable version.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: LLM-based financial modeling, portfolio backtesting, research evaluation
members.background: Nina leads the firm's applied quant research pod and adapted the academic 3S-Trader concept into an internal prototype tested on historical US equity data.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to preserve research fidelity so the discretionary desk sees the framework's adaptive logic rather than a simplified demo, and she is worried that product packaging decisions will quietly strip out the parts that made the results credible.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' should mirror the research workflow closely enough that the desk can judge whether the underlying method actually works in realistic portfolio construction.
A 'weekly package' naturally includes the model-generated score reports, the evolving strategy rationale, and the final selected basket, because those three pieces are the core of 3S-Trader.
When people refer to the DJIA benchmark for this project, they mean the historical constituent set used in the research backtests for each date, not today's static list.
If the first review is due by Friday, that means a reviewable artifact should be ready before market close Friday New York time so stakeholders can discuss it in the weekly desk meeting.

members.name: Ethan Brooks
members.expertise: Internal product launches, stakeholder rollout planning, compliance-ready analytics packaging
members.background: Ethan manages internal pilots for investment tools and has recently been tasked with packaging experimental research outputs into controlled, low-friction workflows for portfolio managers.
members.private_state: He wants a smooth pilot launch with minimal compliance friction and a clean user story for senior stakeholders, and he is concerned that too much research complexity will delay sign-off.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' is a constrained internal rollout that proves usability and governance readiness, not a full reproduction of the research environment.
A 'weekly package' means one concise portfolio recommendation deck with supporting headline rationale, while intermediate research artifacts stay internal unless explicitly requested.
When people say DJIA for an internal business pilot, they mean the current 30-stock tradable universe the desk already recognizes and can review easily.
A Friday deadline means end of day Friday in the shared project tracker, which in practice is acceptable up to late evening as long as the materials are posted before the weekend.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to 'run the pilot' and 'keep the full 3S flow.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the pilot includes all three visible modules as recurring outputs: per-stock scoring reports, strategy revision notes over time, and the final portfolio selection for each cycle.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the pilot includes the internal use of all three modules behind the scenes, but only the final portfolio recommendation plus a short summary needs to be exposed in the client-facing pilot package.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sincerely think 'keeping the full 3S flow' means the method is preserved; neither sees artifact visibility as a separate planning issue because each treats their own scope boundary as the obvious default.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the weekly package
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss sending a 'weekly report' to the desk.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses 'weekly report' to mean a research packet containing stock-level scorecards, the strategy module's updated reasoning, and the selected basket with supporting comparisons.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses 'weekly report' to mean a concise decision memo or slide deck centered on the recommended basket, with only top-line rationale and no stock-by-stock appendix unless needed later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In business settings, 'weekly report' sounds like a routine shared artifact, so both assume the other person has the same standard format in mind and move on to timing and ownership instead of content granularity.

misalignment_points.topic: Which DJIA universe is being used
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to using 'the DJIA set' for the first wave of the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the research universe definition aligned to historical constituent membership over the backtest period so comparisons to prior results remain valid.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the current recognizable DJIA 30 names as of the pilot start date because that is what the discretionary desk expects to see and can review operationally.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The label 'DJIA' is highly familiar and usually treated as self-explanatory, so neither participant expects the other to mean a different constituent set under the same name.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that 'the first version can be ready by Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready by Friday' means a reviewable package finalized before the 4:00 PM ET desk meeting on Friday, with enough completeness to walk through the underlying logic live.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready by Friday' means posted to the project workspace by end of day Friday, even if it lands after the desk meeting and serves as a first asynchronous review version.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same deadline phrase and neither sees the need to specify an exact review event because 'Friday' feels precise enough in normal planning talk unless a scheduling conflict has already surfaced.

turns.inner_thought: I need to anchor this in the actual research logic before packaging starts narrowing it. If the desk is going to judge 3S-Trader, they need to see the full three-part workflow recurring week by week, not just the end basket. Starting with the DJIA set should preserve continuity with the historical constituent definition we used in backtests, otherwise the comparison to prior evidence gets muddy immediately.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. I want to use this to lock the six-week plan for 3S-Trader so we can run the pilot in a way that keeps the full 3S flow visible to the desk, starting with the DJIA set and then layering in the sector basket.

turns.inner_thought: That framing works as long as 'keep the full 3S flow' doesn't mean exposing every research artifact. For the pilot, I need a controlled rollout that feels simple, reviewable, and easy for compliance to bless. A weekly report the desk can scan quickly is the right interface; the deeper machinery can stay behind the scenes unless somebody asks.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I'm aligned on running the pilot and keeping the full 3S flow, but I'd like us to keep the experience lightweight for stakeholders and make sure there's a weekly report the desk can consume without a lot of friction.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Then research can own the recurring outputs from all three modules each cycle: the per-name scoring, the strategy evolution, and the final selection. That's what makes the weekly report useful rather than decorative. If those pieces are there, the desk can actually see how the framework adapts instead of treating it like a black box stock picker.
turns.utterance: That works. My team can own the scoring summaries, strategy updates, and selection outputs each week so the weekly report reflects how the framework is adapting rather than just showing an endpoint.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect: research generates the underlying material, and I turn it into a single clean desk-facing package. I want the story to land on the recommended basket and a crisp rationale, not a dense packet. turns.utterance: Great. On my side, I'll package the weekly report into a concise desk-facing artifact and keep the story centered on the recommended basket and rationale so it lands cleanly with the PMs.

turns.inner_thought: I should reinforce why DJIA comes first: the research evidence is interpretable only if we're talking about the same historical universe definition used in the backtests at each point in time. That's the cleanest bridge from prototype to pilot and gives us a credible baseline before we branch into the sector basket.
turns.utterance: For sequencing, I'd strongly prefer we start with the DJIA set first. It gives us continuity with the prior research evidence and makes the first wave of the pilot much easier to interpret.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. The current DJIA 30 is exactly the kind of recognizable universe that helps the desk engage quickly. Familiar names, easy operational review, low confusion. Once they see something in that frame, adding the sector basket will feel like an extension rather than another moving part.
turns.utterance: I agree, DJIA is the right entry point. The desk will like seeing familiar names there before we add the sector basket, and it keeps the first wave easy to position.

turns.inner_thought: If we front-load the scoring reports and strategy notes, we can have a genuinely reviewable packet ready before the Friday desk meeting. That's important because I want them reacting to the model's logic live, not skimming something after hours. The weekly report should be complete enough to walk through before market close.
turns.utterance: Timing-wise, I think the first version can be ready by Friday if my team prioritizes the scorecards and strategy rationale early in the week, which should put the weekly report on solid footing.

turns.inner_thought: Friday is fine if the research content lands in the workspace by end of day. I can then assemble the pilot materials that evening if needed and still count us on schedule. It doesn't need to make the desk meeting as long as the first version is posted before the weekend and stakeholders can review asynchronously.
turns.utterance: Friday works for me. If the content is in the workspace by end of day, I can turn it around into the pilot materials and we should still be in good shape on the first version.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then once the first weekly report exists, the desk can compare the stock-level scores, the strategy's updated reasoning, and the final picks side by side. That's the whole point of preserving fidelity: they should be able to inspect how the framework moved from signal formation to portfolio choice over the week.
turns.utterance: Exactly. Once the first weekly report is in place, the desk should be able to compare what came through the process with the final picks and see how the strategy shifted over the cycle.

turns.inner_thought: That's a good narrative, and I can present it in a controlled way without opening up the entire research stack. Best split is that Nina's team owns the model outputs and I own the readout format, stakeholder framing, and governance wrapper. That keeps accountability clear and avoids endless edits on presentation materials.

We'll run the DJIA universe first using the same basis as the research setup, get that reviewed Friday afternoon, and only then move to the sector basket.
